title: What I Learned at EDUCAUSE about the Higher Ed AI Conversation(s) Part 3
author: Lance Eaton
summary: In the final part of his EDUCAUSE reflections, Lance Eaton sorts the conference's generative AI conversations into three linked problems: access, cost and equity. He argues that institutions will end up with very different tiers of AI, with elite universities building institutional systems while community colleges settle for bundled copilots. The way a university is organised, centralised or decentralised, will shape who pays for usage and who gets how much. Eaton predicts a new kind of digital divide based on what kind of access people have, not whether they have any. He then ties this to the higher-education mission of producing and disseminating knowledge, drawing on his dissertation work on academic piracy, and warns that AI will speed up research most for the already well-resourced.
points: Access to generative AI in higher education will be layered, with institutional systems for wealthy schools and copilots for poorer ones, much like cable bundles.
Cost and usage models (equal, proportional, or pay-what-you-can-afford) depend on whether a school's structure is centralised or decentralised, and the choice is still open.
The new digital divide is about the quality and level of access, not simply access versus none.
Because AI speeds research and synthesis, it will compound the existing knowledge-access advantage of highly resourced institutions.
quotes: Currently, generative AI is costly to operate at an institutional scale. Who is going to pay for what? Who gets how much usage?

Here, as I mentioned in part 2 is where we will see a new level of differing access in higher education. Some institutions will have institutional-wide AI systems and some will have copilots. Inevitably, Ivy League institutions will get their own institutional AI tools while places like community colleges will end up with copilots.

This process of figuring out the finance of generative AI will like create a new kind of digital divide. It’s not going to be people who have access and don’t have access but what kind of access do you have?
This will extend an increasing inequity of higher education that will allow the benefits to further accrue in elite institutions while other institutions will struggle to keep up.
Higher education’s two central goals are to create knowledge (research) and to disseminate it (teach).

Somehow (ok, I know how, but it’s 60+ pages of my dissertation), higher education has created this system where it pays scholars to produce research, those scholars give that research away to publishers, and publishers sell it at unaffordable rates back to higher ed.
